questions.question: Which stack operation reports the top element without removing it?
questions.explanation: peek() only inspects the top; pop(), poll() and remove() all detach the element from the stack.

questions.question: Calling pop() on a stack that currently holds no elements is which classic error condition?
questions.explanation: Underflow is removing from an empty stack; overflow is pushing beyond a fixed capacity.

questions.question: Which feature is most naturally modelled by a stack?
questions.explanation: Back navigation returns to the most recently visited page first, which is exactly LIFO behaviour.

questions.question: A stack is backed by an array that doubles its capacity when full. What is the cost of one push?
questions.explanation: Most pushes are constant time, but a push that triggers a resize copies all n elements; doubling spreads that cost to O(1) amortized.

questions.question: Why do modern Java style guides prefer ArrayDeque over java.util.Stack?
options: Stack extends Vector and synchronizes every operation
questions.explanation: Stack inherits Vector's index-based API and per-call locking, which is unnecessary overhead; ArrayDeque is unsynchronized and purpose-built.

questions.question: In ArrayDeque, push(e) is exactly equivalent to which call?
questions.explanation: Deque.push is defined as addFirst, so the stack top lives at the head; add and offerLast both append at the tail.

questions.question: A recursive method with no reachable base case eventually fails with which Java error?
questions.explanation: Every call pushes a frame onto the thread's call stack; when that fixed-size stack is exhausted the JVM throws StackOverflowError.

questions.question: What happens when the last line runs?
questions.explanation: java.util.Stack.pop() calls peek(), which throws EmptyStackException when the underlying Vector is empty.

questions.question: What happens when the last line runs?
questions.explanation: ArrayDeque.pop() delegates to removeFirst(), which throws NoSuchElementException; EmptyStackException belongs only to java.util.Stack.

questions.explanation: peek() and poll() signal emptiness by returning null; element() and remove() are the throwing counterparts.

questions.question: Comparing a linked-node stack with a growable-array stack, which statement is true?
options: Both push in O(1); only the array may copy on growth
The linked version needs O(n) time to push
The array version needs O(n) time to pop
The linked version has better cache locality
questions.explanation: Linked push is O(1) worst case, array push is O(1) amortized with an occasional copy; contiguous arrays give better locality, not worse.

questions.question: A bracket-matching scan reaches the end of the string with a non-empty stack. What does that tell you?
options: There were too many closing brackets
The scan must restart from the end
Some opening brackets were never closed
questions.explanation: Leftover openers on the stack were never matched by a closer, so the string is unbalanced; excess closers instead fail earlier on an empty stack.

questions.question: Evaluated with a stack, what is the value of the postfix expression 5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -?
An editor keeps an undo stack and a redo stack. What must happen to the redo stack when the user makes a fresh edit?
options: It must be copied onto the undo stack
It must be swapped with the undo stack
questions.explanation: A new edit starts a new history branch, so the previously undone commands can no longer be validly replayed.

questions.question: Rewriting a recursive DFS to use an explicit ArrayDeque mainly gains you what?
options: The identical visit order for free
Depth limited by heap size, not the thread stack
questions.explanation: The explicit stack lives on the heap, so very deep graphs no longer risk StackOverflowError; the asymptotics are unchanged and the visit order differs unless neighbours are pushed in reverse.

questions.question: Two threads run drain() on the same shared java.util.Stack. Is this code thread-safe?
options: Yes, every Stack method is synchronized
No, the check and the pop are not one atomic step
Yes, provided the field is final
No, because pop() is the only unsynchronized method
questions.explanation: Each method locks individually, but another thread can empty the stack between isEmpty() and pop(), so pop() can still throw EmptyStackException.

questions.question: Using standard shunting-yard rules, what is the postfix form of a + b * c - d?
questions.explanation: * has higher precedence, so b c * is emitted first, then + joins a, and finally - applies d.

questions.question: In the classic next-greater-element scan, what invariant does the monotonic stack keep?
options: Values non-increasing from bottom to top
Values non-decreasing from bottom to top
Every index seen so far, in input order
Values re-sorted ascending after each push
questions.explanation: Each new element pops every smaller value, since that new element is their next greater one, leaving the remaining values non-increasing toward the top.

questions.question: Largest rectangle in a histogram solved with a monotonic stack runs in what time?
options: O(n log n) because of stack maintenance
O(n) total, as each index is pushed and popped once
O(n^2) worst case, e.g. a decreasing histogram
O(n) only when all bar heights are distinct
questions.explanation: Every index enters and leaves the stack at most once, so the total work over the whole scan is linear regardless of the shape of the input.

questions.question: Which comparison replaces ? so getMin() stays correct when the same minimum is pushed twice?
questions.explanation: With <= each copy of the minimum gets its own entry in mins, so popping one copy does not lose the minimum that is still in data.

questions.question: On HotSpot Java 17, what happens to deeply tail-recursive code?
options: javac rewrites tail calls into loops
The JIT removes tail frames after warm-up
No tail-call elimination, so it still overflows the stack
questions.explanation: Neither javac nor HotSpot performs tail-call elimination, so every call keeps its frame and deep recursion throws StackOverflowError.
